topics.title: India-China border
bullets: China has recently established a new administrative county named “Cenling” in the Xinjiang region, located near Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and the Afghanistan border, highlighting its growing focus on strategically sensitive frontier areas.
The move represents the third such administrative restructuring in a short span, reflecting a broader pattern of strengthening governance and control over disputed and border regions.
Alongside ongoing renaming attempts in Arunachal Pradesh, this reflects China’s broader strategy to reinforce territorial claims. Aksai Chin Dispute –

During the 19th century, Aksai Chin became a contested region between British India and Qing China, with different boundary proposals such as the Johnson Line and the Macartney- MacDonald Line creating ambiguity over territorial claims.
The Johnson Line placed Aksai Chin within the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir under British India, forming the basis of India’s present-day claim over the region.
However, the lack of a clearly demarcated boundary and absence of effective control led to continued uncertainty regarding sovereignty over Aksai Chin.
After India’s independence in 1947, Aksai Chin was considered part of the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir, but China gradually established control over the region in the 1950s.
China constructed a strategic road (G219 highway) connecting Xinjiang to Tibet through Aksai Chin, significantly increasing the region’s military and logistical importance.

The dispute escalated into the 1962 Sino-Indian War, after which China retained control over Aksai Chin, making it a continuing point of conflict between the two countries. The China- Arunachal border dispute -
After India’s independence in 1947, the state now known as Arunachal Pradesh was called North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) and administered by the state of Assam.
However, it was not until after 25 years that the erstwhile NEFA became a Union Territory and named Arunachal Pradesh.
On February 20, 1987, it was declared a full-fledged state.
In 1987, the Indian Government as per the 53rd Amendment of the Indian Constitution a year prior declared the extreme northern part of the country the 24th state of Union India.
The state is known as the ‘land of the rising sun’ (not to be confused with Japan). India and China border –
Arunachal Pradesh is also home to the Line of Actual Control (LAC), arguably one of the heavily contested borders, after the meaning of its name ‘land of the dawn-lit mountains’.

India shares a 3488 km border with China which is divided into three sectors – 1. the eastern sector (along the states of Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim) 2. the western sector (Ladakh) 3. the middle sector (Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh)

topics.title: India-China border
bullets: However, Beijing only considers the LAC to be around 2,000 km.
The ill-defined border along these sectors has caused many disputes over the years between the two countries.
Even after India gained independence, the borders, which were internationally agreed upon, remained the same over the years.
Beijing believes that these "unequal treaties" had been imposed on it during its “century of humiliation” and called for re- negotiation of all the borders with India.
This includes the arbitrary one drawn by British officials based primarily on the highest watershed principle.
In the eastern sector (Arunachal Pradesh & Sikkim area), the border was drawn along the McMahon Line which was named after Sir Henry McMahon, foreign secretary of British India.
After the 1911 uprising ended imperialist rule in China, the newly founded Republic of China lacked the strength to assert its demands at the negotiation table.
Moreover, Tibet acknowledged China's suzerainty (limited self- rule) until the 1911 revolution. However, following the revolution, Tibet declared de facto independence, which China did not accept.
In 1914 the 890 km border between erstwhile British India and Tibet was decided at the Simla Convention between China, Tibet and Great Britain.
The final draft of Simla convention was only signed by Sir Henry McMahon and Paljor Dorje Shatra, the Dalai Lama-appointed representative of Tibet.
Chen I-fen, the Chinese representative, contested the new line, saying Tibet was not an independent country and did not have the authority to decide its border.
Despite drawing the McMahon Line, the British largely stayed out of Tawang, leaving it to be controlled by Lhasa, the Tibetan capital.
The People's Republic of China was established by Mao Zedong in 1949, and it was followed by the annexation of Tibet by the People's Liberation Army in 1950, shortly after India's Independence.
Beijing argued that when the agreement came into effect, it was signed by the Tibetan government, which was not a sovereign state at the time.
Consequently, China claims parts of Arunachal Pradesh, including Tawang, as a part of Tibet. What are fishtails?
Fishtail 1 in the Dibang Valley and Fishtail 2 in the Anjaw district are in the easternmost corner of Arunachal Pradesh.
Arunachal Pradesh's Fishtails area, named after the distinctive shape of its boundary line, is made up of Fishtail 1 and Fishtail 2.

While Fish Tail-I is largely glaciated with sparse patrolling, Indian and Chinese troops had previously launched patrolling in the Fish Tail-II region in coordination with one another. Source: NORTHEAST NOW Earlier clashes -

In a 1959 note to Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai first mentioned the term 'Line of Actual Control' (LAC), defining it as the "line up to which each side exercises actual control".
However, Nehru rejected this concept as "incoherent".
The situation worsened when Beijing released an official map showing parts of Arunachal Pradesh as Chinese territory.
This move sparked the Sino-Indian War in 1962.
Chinese troops surrounded Indian posts in Ladakh and the North-East Frontier Agency (now known as Arunachal Pradesh) in August 1962.
On November 20, China announced a unilateral ceasefire and soon afterwards withdrew from most of the invaded area, retaining control of about 14,700 square miles of territory in Aksai Chin.
After the 1962 war, the LAC became an informal cease-fire line between India and China.
However, The LAC is an ambiguous border, seen as a subjective concept by both countries, often leading to disagreement.
India considers the McMahon line as its version of the LAC, while China claims Aksai Chin and Arunachal Pradesh, which it refers to as ' Zangnan, South Tibet', as its territory.
According to reports, in 1975 four Indian Army personnel were killed after an ambush by the Chinese military in Arunachal Pradesh’s Tulung La region.
According to reports, there was a five-hour confrontation between some 600 military personnel from both sides who engaged in hand- to-hand combat, in June 2020.
At least 20 Indian soldiers were killed and while China claims that only four of their soldiers died, the death toll is speculated to be over 40 PLA troops, as per media reports.
In December 2022, the two sides again engaged in a clash this time at the Yangtse, Tawang in Arunachal Pradesh.
The incident took place on December 9 following which Beijing alleged that Indian troops “illegally” crossed the LAC.
The Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh in his statement to the parliament said China attempted to “unilaterally change the status quo”.
In an intensified effort to emphasise its claim over India’s Arunachal Pradesh, China came up with a third set of names for 11 places in Arunachal Pradesh in August 2023.
This is Beijing’s third such list on Arunachal Pradesh, attempting to “rename” places by giving them what it calls “standardised geographical names”.
Earlier China’s civil affairs ministry issued The first batch of six places announced in 2017 and the second batch of 15 places in 2021. Resolving border disputes -
The Agreement on the Maintenance of Peace and Tranquillity was signed on 7 September 1993.
It called for a renunciation of the use of force, recognition of the LAC, and the resolution of the border issue through negotiations.
The Agreement on Confidence Building Measures in the Military Field along the Line of Actual Control in the India- China Border Areas was signed on 29 November 1996.
It laid down pledges on non-aggression, prior notification of large troop movements, and exchange of maps to resolve disagreements over the LAC.
Reaffirming the Declaration on Principles for Relations and Comprehensive Cooperation between India and China was signed on 23 June 2003.
The Border Defence Co-operation Agreement was signed in 2013 following the Depsang Valley incident.
The Panchsheel Agreement was a set of five principles to govern relations between India and China which was signed in 1954.
The agreement’s slogans include “Hindi-Chini Bhai Bhai” and “Asia for Asians.”

It was signed by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru and Premier Zhou Enlai. Agreement based on the following principles: - 1. Mutual respect for each other’s territorial integrity and sovereignty 2. Mutual non-aggression 3. Mutual non-interference 4. Equality and mutual benefit 5. Peaceful co-existence.” Recent Developments –
India has strongly rejected China’s latest move to assign new names to places, terming it a “mischievous attempt” to assert unfounded territorial claims.
The Ministry of External Affairs described these as “fictitious names” and emphasised that such attempts to create false and baseless narratives cannot alter the ground reality.
The development, along with China’s recent administrative actions in border regions, reflects a broader strategy to reinforce its territorial assertions through symbolic and structural measures.
The newly created Cenling county is located near the Karakoram mountain range, in close proximity to Pakistan- occupied Kashmir and Afghanistan.
Its location enhances its geopolitical significance, particularly in terms of border security and regional connectivity.
The move raises concerns regarding increased Chinese presence in sensitive frontier regions.
The administrative centre Kashgar, under which the new county falls, is a historically significant city and serves as a major hub connecting China with South and Central Asia.
It is also the starting point of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, a major infrastructure project that passes through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.
India has consistently opposed this corridor on the grounds that it violates its sovereignty and territorial integrity, making it a key point of contention.
Prior to the creation of “Cenling”, China had established two new counties named “Hean” and “Hekang” in the Xinjiang region as part of its administrative expansion strategy.
India had formally protested these developments, stating that parts of the jurisdiction of these counties fall within its Union Territory of Ladakh.
“Hean” reportedly includes a significant portion of the Aksai Chin plateau, which remains a key point of dispute between India and China.

topics.title: India’s Nuclear Era
bullets: India took a significant step towards energy independence on 6 April 2026, when the indigenously designed and built Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu attained first criticality.
This moment marked the start of a sustained and controlled nuclear chain reaction in the 500 MWe reactor, a technology India has pursued for decades.
With this achievement, the country formally entered the second stage of the three-stage nuclear power programme envisioned by Homi J Bhabha. Homi Bhabha’s three-state nuclear program –
India’s nuclear journey began shortly after Independence with the establishment of the Atomic Energy Commission in 1948.
In 1956, Asia’s first research reactor, Apsara, was commissioned at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in Trombay.
2. India was the second Asian nation to build a nuclear power plant in 1969 at Tarapur, just after Japan and long before China.
It also built up an impressive nuclear research and development programme in the 1950s and 1960s with significant assistance from its Western partners.

India owes the vision of the three-phase programme of nuclear power to ensure energy security to Dr Homi J Bhabha, the father of India’s nuclear programme, and Dr Vikram Sarabhai, who recognised the need for developing (Fast Breeder Reactor) FBRs, as these reactors generate more nuclear fuel than they consume due to the gainful conversion of fertile isotopes into fissile material. → STAGE 1:
Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) use natural uranium-based fuels to generate electricity, while producing fissile plutonium (Pu239), which can be extracted by reprocessing the spent fuel.
It uses heavy water (deuterium oxide) both as a coolant and moderator.
The programme has been supplemented by the construction of imported Light Water Reactors (LWRs). About Uranium –
Uranium is a naturally occurring radioactive element, which has the atomic number of 92 and corresponds to the chemical symbol U in the periodic table.
It belongs to a special group of elements called “actinides” — elements that were discovered relatively late in history.
Uranium is “radioactive”, which means it decays over time and releases energy in the process. Its special properties make uranium the main source of fuel for nuclear reactors.
Uranium is among the more common elements in the earth’s crust — about 500 times more common than gold.
There are three natural isotopes of uranium — uranium-234 (U- 234), uranium-235 (U-235) and uranium-238 (U-238).
U-235 is needed for the nuclear fuel, however, uranium typically contains only 0.72% of U-235 and to increase the concentration, enrichment is done.
India has around 76,000 tonnes of uranium reserves.
Government data suggests these deposits could only support about 10,000 MW of nuclear power generation for around 30 years.
India had signed a landmark civil nuclear deal with the United States in 2008 under then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and US President Barack Obama.
India and Canada last year agreed to cooperate in uranium supplies, renewable energy, LPG sector, nuclear technology, and advanced reactors.
Both countries will work together to build Small Modular Reactors. These are small, factory-built nuclear plants that are much safer and cheaper than giant traditional plants.

A new joint center will open in Mumbai to research how to safely dispose of nuclear waste. Canadian engineers will help fix and upgrade India’s older power plants so they can safely run for another 20 to 30 years.
Before this, in 2015, PM Narendra Modi has signed the Uranium Supply Agreement with Cameo for supply of Uranium ore during the period of 2015-20.
An agreement between the Government of India and the Government of Canada for Cooperation in Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy was signed on 27.06.2010.
India has a strict law called the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act. It states that if an accident happens, the foreign supplier has to pay heavy fines. → STAGE 2:
The plutonium obtained from Stage 1 is used as fuel in Fast Breeder Reactors, which generate more fuel than they consume. The PFBR at Kalpakkam marks India's entry into this stage.

It involves setting up Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs) of the kind at Kalpakkam, using plutonium-based fuels, which can enhance nuclear power capacity, and convert fertile thorium into fissile uranium (U233).
Reprocessing of the spent fuel is vital for efficient utilisation of the plutonium inventory. About Thorium –

Thorium was discovered by Jons Jakob Berzelius. Thorium is a weakly radioactive, naturally occurring metal found in soil and rocks, identified as a promising, abundant, and safer alternative to uranium for nuclear power.
It is "fertile" rather than "fissile," meaning it must be converted into uranium-233 in a reactor to produce energy, offering potentially lower, shorter-lived nuclear waste.
India holds limited uranium reserves but one of the largest thorium reserves in the world. → STAGE 3:
The third stage will be based on the ThU233 cycle.
U233 produced in the second stage can be used for the third stage of the power programme, which consists of advanced thermal and fast breeder reactors, for long-term energy security.
The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is proposed for this. Now, the use of molten salt reactors is also seen as an option. The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam -
The vital second stage of India’s three-stage nuclear programme got a boost with the country’s first indigenous Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR) at Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu attaining criticality.

Attaining criticality, or going critical, means the initiation of a self- sustaining nuclear fission reaction that will eventually lead to the generation of power by the 500-megawatt electric (MWe) FBR.

Attaining criticality is a key milestone before full power generation, indicating that the reactor core is functioning as designed and that each fission event in the core now releases a sufficient number of neutrons to sustain an ongoing series of reactions.

A little over two years ago, the completion of ‘core loading’, or the process of placing nuclear fuel assemblies inside the core of a nuclear reactor, was completed in March 2024 in case of the Kalpakkam FBR.

This reactor will initially use uranium-plutonium mixed oxide (MOX) fuel, with a ‘blanket’ of a Uranium isotope (U238) around the fuel core that will undergo nuclear transmutation to produce more fuel – therefore, the name ‘breeder’.
Nuclear transmutation involves the conversion of a chemical element or isotope into another chemical element, with the numbers of protons or neutrons in the nucleus of the atom undergoing a change.

The PFBR represents decades of indigenous research, design, and engineering. Its technology was developed by the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), an R&D centre under the Department of Atomic Energy.

The reactor is designed to eventually use Thorium-232 in the blanket. Through transmutation, Thorium-232 will be converted into Uranium-233, the fuel that will power India's third stage of nuclear energy based on thorium.

The spent fuel generated by the PFBR will be reprocessed and recycled back into the reactor. This closes the second-stage fuel cycle and paves the way for large-scale use of India's abundant thorium reserves in Stage 3.
Once operational, India will be only the second country after Russia to run a commercial FBR, while many countries have discontinued such programmes due to safety concerns.

This unique capability significantly enhances the utilization of nuclear fuel resources and enables the country to extract far greater energy from its limited uranium reserves while also preparing for large-scale use of thorium in the future. India’s nuclear landscape –
India's current nuclear capacity is 8.78 Gigawatt (GW). In 2024–25, nuclear power plants generated 56,681 Million Units of electricity across the country.
Nuclear power has consistently accounted for around 3% of India's total electricity generation. In 2024–25, its share stood at 3.1%.

India's nuclear capacity is set to grow nearly 3x in the coming years. With indigenous 700 Megawatt (MW) reactors and 1,000 MW reactors being developed through international cooperation, the installed capacity is projected to reach 22.38 GW by 2031–32.
India has signed Inter-Governmental Agreements (IGAs) on Civil Nuclear Cooperation for peaceful purposes with 18 countries, reflecting the growing global confidence in India's nuclear programme.
The Government has announced the Nuclear Energy Mission, outlined in the Union Budget 2025–26, with the aim of achieving 100 GW of nuclear power generation capacity by 2047.
The mission also supports India's broader goal of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2070.

The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is leading the development of next-generation reactor designs, including the 200 MWe Bharat Small Modular Reactor (BSMR-200), the 55 MWe SMR-55, and a High-Temperature Gas-Cooled Reactor of up to 5 MWth (Megawatt thermal) designed for hydrogen generation.
Currently India has 22 nuclear power reactors operating in 6 states with the largest being in Kundankulam Power Plant, Tamil Nadu.
The establishment procedures and utilizations were earlier given in the Atomic Energy Act, 1962. SHANTI Act –

The Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India Act, 2025 (passed December 2025) revolutionizes India’s nuclear sector by ending the state monopoly, allowing private and foreign firms to build/operate plants.
It repealed the Atomic Energy Act (AEA), 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act (CLNDA), 2010.

Establishes an Atomic Energy Redressal Advisory Council to facilitate the redressal of disputes. Also provides for a dedicated Commission to handle cases involving severe nuclear damage and ensure timely adjudication.
The Appellate Tribunal for Electricity, set up under the Electricity Act, 2003, will serve as the appellate authority.

Certain sensitive nuclear fuel-cycle activities are reserved exclusively for Central Government or its wholly owned institutions. These include enrichment of radioactive substances, management of spent fuel, etc.

Introduces a clear graded liability system for nuclear operators. Liability caps: ₹3,000 crore (large plants), ₹1,500 crore (medium), ₹100 crore (SMRs). Government bears liability beyond the cap through a Nuclear Liability Fund.
